docs.title: JsonPreprocessor
docs.text:
JSON with superpowers - comments, imports, parameters and more.

The JsonPreprocessor is a Python package that reads JSON files written in an extended JSON format (called JSONP) and returns a plain Python dictionary. It is made for projects that need to maintain large and structured sets of configuration parameters.

flowchart LR
    A["config.jsonp<br/>(comments, imports,<br/>parameters, ...)"] --> B(["JsonPreprocessor"])
    C["common.jsonp"] -.imported by.-> A
    B --> D["Python dictionary<br/>(DotDict)"]

docs.title: What you can do with JSONP
docs.text: Feature Example Learn more Comments // a comment, /* block */ Comments Import other files "[import]" : "./common.jsonp" Import of JSON files Reference parameters "b" : ${a} Overwriting parameters Overwrite values ${dict}['key'] : 42 Overwriting parameters dotdict notation ${dict.key.sub_key} dotdict notation Python keywords True, False, None Boolean and null values Python inline code <<${A} + ${B}>> Python inline code Byte values b'\x41\x42' Byte sequences

docs.title: A first impression
docs.text:
{
   // common values are maintained in one place only
   "[import]" : "./common.jsonp",

   "device"   : "Device_01",
   "timeout"  : 30,
   "greeting" : "Hello ${device}!",

   // overwrite a value that was defined in common.jsonp
   ${limits}['max_retries'] : 5
}

from JsonPreprocessor.CJsonPreprocessor import CJsonPreprocessor

values = CJsonPreprocessor().jsonLoad("./config.jsonp")
print(values.greeting)          # Hello Device_01!

docs.title: class CJsonPreprocessor
docs.text:
Extends the JSON syntax by the following features:

  • c/c++-style comments within JSON files
  • import of JSON files into JSON files
  • definition and usage of parameters within JSON files
  • Python keywords True, False and None

docs.title: Constructor
docs.text:
CJsonPreprocessor(syntax=CSyntaxType.python, current_cfg={}, key_pattern=r'.+')
Argument Type Default Description syntax CSyntaxType CSyntaxType.python If set to python, Python keywords are allowed as part of JSON files. current_cfg dict {} Parameters which are available in addition to the parameters of the JSONP file. They can be referenced and overwritten and are part of the result. key_pattern str r'.+' Regular expression (module regex) all key names must match. See User defined naming convention.

Raises an Exception if key_pattern is not a string, is empty, is '.*' or contains only whitespace.

docs.title: jsonLoad(json_file) / json_load(json_file)
docs.text:
Entry point of the JsonPreprocessor. Loads the JSONP file, preprocesses it and returns the result as Python dictionary.

Argument Type Description json_file str Path and name of the main JSONP file. The path can be absolute or relative (to the executed script) and may contain environment variables.

Returns: DotDict - the preprocessed JSONP file(s) as Python dictionary.

Raises: Exception in case of any error.

docs.title: jsonLoads(jsonp_content, reference_dir=None) / json_loads(...)
docs.text:
Loads JSONP content from a string, preprocesses it and returns the result as Python dictionary.

Argument Type Default Description jsonp_content str - The JSONP content. reference_dir str None Reference directory for imported files with relative paths. Must exist.

Returns: DotDict - the preprocessed JSONP content as Python dictionary.

Raises: Exception if the content is not a string, the reference directory does not exist, or in case of any error in the content.

docs.title: jsonDump(json_obj, out_file) / json_dump(...)
docs.text:
Writes the content of a Python dictionary to a file in standard JSON format (UTF-8, indentation 4).

Argument Type Description json_obj dict The dictionary to be written. out_file str Path and name of the JSON output file. The path can be absolute or relative (to the executed script) and may contain environment variables.

Returns: str - normalized path and name of the written JSON file.

Raises: Exception if the file cannot be written.

docs.title: The DotDict return type
docs.text: All loading methods return a DotDict (package pydotdict): a dict subclass that additionally provides attribute access to keys (values.key.sub_key). Nested dictionaries are also of type DotDict. If the JSONP content is not a JSON object (e.g. a list), the plain Python value is returned.

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Do I have to use the extension .jsonp?

No. The JsonPreprocessor also accepts .json files. But the extension .jsonp is recommended to have a strict separation between standard JSON and the extended format - and to get the right syntax highlighting (see VSCodium support).

Is every JSON file also a valid JSONP file?

Yes. See Standard JSON format.

Can I convert a JSONP configuration back to standard JSON?

Yes. Load it with jsonLoad and write the result with jsonDump. The written file contains standard JSON with all imports, parameters and inline code resolved. See Using the JsonPreprocessor in Python.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
Why does a parameter not have the value I expect?

The value a parameter has finally depends on the order of definitions, redefinitions and imports - the definition processed last wins. Check whether an import placed after your definition overwrites it. See The order matters.

Can I reference a parameter that is defined later in the file?

Yes. Parameters can be referenced independently of the position of their definition, as long as they are defined somewhere in the configuration and the references are not cyclic.

Why is my number a string?

You probably used quotes: "b" : "${a}" converts the value to str. Use "b" : ${a} to keep the data type.

How can I add an element to a list?

Adding elements to an existing list on the left-hand side is not possible. Overwrite the entire list instead, e.g. ${my_list} : <<${my_list} + ["new"]>>. See Python inline code.

I made a typo in a key name, but I get no error.

With implicit creation the missing levels of a data structure are created automatically - also for misspelled names. Check the result (e.g. with jsonDump) or restrict the key names with a naming convention.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Is it safe to load JSONP files from unknown sources?

No. Python inline code is executed while loading a file. Only load JSONP files from trusted sources.

docs.title: Robot Framework
docs.text:
Can I use JSONP files in Robot Framework tests?

Yes - with the RobotFramework_TestsuitesManagement (part of RobotFramework AIO). There, parameter names are restricted to letters, digits and underscores.

docs.text:
The component test is the main regression test. Every test case (JPP_xxxx) is configured in test/testconfig/TestConfig.py with the input file in test/testfiles/ and the expected result (EXPECTEDRETURN) or the expected exception (EXPECTEDEXCEPTION).

cd test
python component_test.py                         # all test cases
python component_test.py --testid="JPP_0201"     # a single test case
python component_test.py --testid="JPP_0201;JPP_0202"

The overview of all test cases is available in test/JPP_TestUsecases.html (also .csv, .rst, .txt). Further options are described in test/readme.rst.

docs.title: CJsonPreprocessor.py - the facade
docs.text:
The only module users import. It validates the constructor arguments, creates an ImportResolver per call and drives the processing pipeline.

Member Responsibility __init__(syntax, current_cfg, key_pattern) validates and stores the options json_load / jsonLoad file entry point json_loads / jsonLoads string entry point, optional reference_dir json_dump / jsonDump writes standard JSON __process expansion loop for dynamic imports and final interpreter run getVersion, getVersionDate version information from version.py

For backward compatibility the module also re-exports the helper classes of common.py (CSyntaxType, CNameMangling, CPythonJSONDecoder, CKeyChecker, CTreeNode, CTextProcessor).

docs.title: Architecture at a glance
docs.text:
The JsonPreprocessor is built like a small compiler: the text is parsed into an abstract syntax tree (AST), imports are expanded on AST level, and an interpreter evaluates the tree into Python data.

    end

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text: Principle Implementation Separation of syntax and semantics Parsing (jsonp_parser, dollar_syntax) produces a pure data structure (AST); all semantics live in the interpreter. JSON compatibility The parser follows the scanner of the Python standard library (json.decoder), so that JSON syntax errors keep the well known messages and positions. Imports on AST level An import is replaced by the members of the imported file - no text concatenation, every member keeps its origin for error messages. Order independent references Values are evaluated lazily, therefore a parameter can be referenced before it is defined. One error type internally All modules raise JsonpError; the facade converts it into a plain Exception (public contract). Stable public API CJsonPreprocessor keeps the historical camel case methods as wrappers of the snake case methods.

docs.title: 1. Loading and comment removal
docs.text:
ImportResolver.load_file reads the file and calls CTextProcessor.load_and_remove_comments, which removes // line comments and /* */ block comments (strings are respected). Parsed files are cached per resolver, so a file that is imported several times is parsed only once.

check_reserved_tokens rejects content that contains internal marker tokens (CNameMangling).

docs.title: 2. Text preparation
docs.text:
prepare_text (in jsonp_parser.py) works line by line on the comment free text:

  • removes empty lines and trailing whitespace,
  • checks the quotation of every line (shlex),
  • rejects Python inline code inside dollar operator expressions,
  • normalizes index notation ([+1] → [1], [ 'key' ] → ['key']) and Unicode digits.

docs.title: 3. Parsing into an AST
docs.text:
JsonpParser is a recursive scanner modeled after json.decoder. In addition to standard JSON it recognizes the JSONP extensions and produces these node types:

classDiagram
    class Obj {
        members
    }
    class Member {
        key
        value
        origin
    }
    class Import {
        value
        source
        pos
        is_static()
    }
    class Arr {
        items
    }
    class DollarKey {
        text
        ref
    }
    class Value {
        <<abstract>>
    }
    Obj "1" *-- "*" Member
    Obj "1" *-- "*" Import
    Member --> DollarKey : key (optional)
    Member --> Value : value
    Arr "1" *-- "*" Value
    Value <|-- Scalar
    Value <|-- Str
    Value <|-- Bare
    Value <|-- Inline
    Value <|-- Bytes
    Value <|-- Obj
    Value <|-- Arr

(Value is not a real class - it stands for any node that can be used as a value.)

JSONP construct AST node { ... } Obj [ ... ] Arr 1, true, None Scalar "text" / "text ${a}" Str (with parts if it contains references) ${a}[0] (unquoted value) Bare << ... >> Inline b'...' Bytes "[import]" : ... / "[import?]" : ... Import (path, condition, alternative, optional) ${a}['k'] : ... (key) Member with DollarKey

Dollar operator expressions are parsed by DollarParser (dollar_syntax.py) into Ref objects:

template  := ( text | ref )*
ref       := '${' name '}' index*
name      := ( name_char | ref )+          -- nested references are allowed
index     := '[' ws* ( int | "'" template "'" | ref ) ws* ']'

Dotted names (${a.b.0}) are kept as plain name text in the AST - splitting them into path segments requires runtime knowledge (a key may itself contain a dot) and is done by the interpreter.

docs.title: 4. Import expansion
docs.text:
ImportResolver.expand returns a copy of the AST in which every import with a known path is replaced by the members of the imported file:

flowchart LR
    subgraph before["AST of main.jsonp"]
        direction TB
        m1["Member a"] --> i1["Import ./common.jsonp"] --> m2["Member b"]
    end
    subgraph after["expanded AST"]
        direction TB
        n1["Member a"] --> c1["Member x (origin common.jsonp)"] --> c2["Member y (origin common.jsonp)"] --> n2["Member b"]
    end
    before -- expand --> after
  • Static paths (plain strings) are resolved immediately, relative to the importing file.
  • Dynamic paths (containing ${...} or <<...>>) stay Import nodes until their value is known.
  • The import chain (list of files from the root to the current file) is used for cyclic import detection.
  • Imported members get the origin attribute (path of the imported file) for correct key ordering and error messages.

docs.title: 5. Resolving dynamic imports
docs.text:
The path of a dynamic import depends on parameters - which may themselves be defined in imported files. Therefore the facade (CJsonPreprocessor.__process) iterates:

sequenceDiagram
    participant F as __process
    participant R as ImportResolver
    participant I as Interpreter (lenient)
    F->>R: expand(tree)
    loop while unresolved imports exist
        F->>I: run(expanded)  [errors ignored]
        I-->>F: resolved paths of dynamic imports
        alt no new paths
            F->>F: stop
        else new paths found
            F->>R: expand(tree, resolved)
        end
    end
    F->>F: final Interpreter run (strict)

The lenient interpreter skips imports that cannot be resolved yet and only records the paths it could compute.

docs.title: 6. Evaluation
docs.text:
The Interpreter evaluates the expanded AST. The root object is the parameter store: every ${...} is resolved against it.

  1. Seeding (seed_object): every object is seeded before its members are executed. Keys are created in their final order (a redefined key moves to the position of its last definition). Values that do not depend on anything are stored immediately; all others are stored as _Lazy placeholders.
  2. Execution (exec_object): members are executed in document order.
  3. literal keys get their (evaluated) value,
  4. dollar keys (${...} : value) overwrite existing values or implicitly create missing dictionaries (assign),
  5. remaining Import nodes (dynamic paths) are loaded and executed in place (exec_import).
  6. Lazy evaluation (force): a _Lazy placeholder is evaluated when it is referenced. This allows references to parameters that are defined later in the document. A placeholder that is referenced during its own evaluation raises _Busy (cyclic reference).
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Lazy: seed (value depends on references)
    [*] --> Value: seed (literal)
    Lazy --> Busy: force()
    Busy --> Value: evaluated
    Busy --> Error: referenced again (cycle)
    Value --> Value: overwritten by dollar key

Python inline code (Inline nodes) is handed to the InlineCodeEvaluator: dollar operator expressions inside the code are translated into accesses to a read-only view of the parameter store (self.jp_globals[...]), then the expression is evaluated. Only results of JSON compatible types are accepted.

docs.title: 7. Result and errors
docs.text: The result dictionary is wrapped into a DotDict. Every error inside the pipeline is a JsonpError (or a subclass like NotAvailable); the public methods convert it into a plain Exception with the same message.

docs.title: Why JSONP?
docs.text:
JSON is a popular format for configuration files: it is simple, human readable and supported by nearly every programming language. But for large projects with many configuration parameters, plain JSON quickly reaches its limits:

  • You cannot add comments to explain the meaning of a parameter.
  • You cannot split a large configuration into several files.
  • You cannot reuse values - the same value has to be written again and again.
  • You cannot overwrite a common value for a specific use case.

The JsonPreprocessor closes these gaps. It extends the JSON format by the following features:

  1. Parts of a JSON file can be commented out.
  2. A JSON file can import other JSON files (also nested imports).
  3. Parameters can be defined, referenced and overwritten (follow-up definitions overwrite previous definitions of the same parameter).
  4. Python keywords like True, False and None can be used in addition to the JSON keywords true, false and null.
  5. Python inline code can be used to compute values.

docs.title: A typical use case
docs.text:
Imagine a software that consists of several components. Every component needs its own set of parameters, but all components also share a common set of parameters.

flowchart TB
    common["common.jsonp<br/><i>parameters used by all components</i>"]
    A["componentA.jsonp<br/><i>parameters of component A</i>"]
    B["componentB.jsonp<br/><i>parameters of component B</i>"]
    common -- "[import]" --> A
    common -- "[import]" --> B
    A --> RA(["JsonPreprocessor"]) --> DA["dictionary for component A"]
    B --> RB(["JsonPreprocessor"]) --> DB["dictionary for component B"]

With JSONP

  • the common parameters are defined only once (in common.jsonp) - no redundancy, easier maintenance,
  • every component file imports the common part and adds its own parameters,
  • a component file can overwrite a common value if it needs a different one,
  • comments explain the meaning of each parameter directly in the file.

Smaller files with a specific content are easier to maintain than a single huge file that contains everything.

docs.title: The file extension .jsonp
docs.text:
The new features cause some deviations from the JSON standard. These deviations harm the syntax highlighting of editors and cause invalid findings of JSON related static code checkers.

To clearly separate the standard format from the extended format, the JsonPreprocessor uses the file extension .jsonp for JSON files in extended format.

Tip

For the editor VSCodium (and VS Code) an extension is available that adds syntax highlighting for .jsonp files. See VSCodium support.

docs.title: Quick start
docs.text: This page guides you through your first JSONP file in three small steps.

docs.title: Step 1 - Write a JSONP file
docs.text:
Create a file config.jsonp:

{
   // general settings
   "project" : "Demo",
   "version" : 1,
   "debug"   : False,

   // a value built from other values
   "title"   : "${project} (version ${version})"
}

This file already uses three JSONP features: a comment (//), the Python keyword False and parameter references (${...}).

docs.title: Step 2 - Load it with Python
docs.text:
Create a script load_config.py next to the JSONP file:

from JsonPreprocessor.CJsonPreprocessor import CJsonPreprocessor
import pprint

json_preprocessor = CJsonPreprocessor()
try:
    values = json_preprocessor.jsonLoad("./config.jsonp")
    pprint.pprint(values)
except Exception as reason:
    print(f"'{reason}'")

The main method of the JsonPreprocessor is jsonLoad. Input is the path and the name of a JSONP file, output is a dictionary containing all values parsed from this file.

Always use try/except

In case of any error in the JSONP file (syntax error, missing file, unknown parameter, ...) the JsonPreprocessor raises an exception. Therefore call jsonLoad inside a try/except block. See Error handling.

docs.title: Step 3 - Run it
docs.text:
python load_config.py

Outcome:

DotDict({'project': 'Demo', 'version': 1, 'debug': False, 'title': 'Demo (version 1)'})

pprint is used to give the output a better readability.

docs.title: Access the values
docs.text:
The returned object is a DotDict - a dictionary that additionally supports attribute access:

print(values['title'])   # standard dictionary access
print(values.title)      # dot notation

docs.title: What happens behind the scenes?
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Your script
    participant J as JsonPreprocessor
    participant F as config.jsonp
    S->>J: jsonLoad("./config.jsonp")
    J->>F: read file
    J->>J: remove comments
    J->>J: resolve imports
    J->>J: resolve parameters ${...}
    J-->>S: DotDict with all values

docs.text:

  • All discussed JSONP examples can be tested with the script from step 2.
  • Keep the Cheat sheet at hand.

docs.title: Boolean and null values
docs.text:
JSON supports the boolean values true and false, and also the null value null. In Python, the corresponding values differ: True, False and None.

Because the JsonPreprocessor is a Python application and therefore the returned content is required to be Python compatible, the JsonPreprocessor does the conversion automatically.

Accepted in JSONP files are both styles:

{
   "param_06" : true,
   "param_07" : false,
   "param_08" : null,
   "param_09" : True,
   "param_10" : False,
   "param_11" : None
}

The output contains all keywords in Python style only:

{'param_06': True,
 'param_07': False,
 'param_08': None,
 'param_09': True,
 'param_10': False,
 'param_11': None}
JSON keyword Python keyword (also allowed in JSONP) Result in Python true True True false False False null None None

Note

The Python keywords are accepted with the default syntax setting CSyntaxType.python. See Using the JsonPreprocessor in Python.

docs.title: Byte sequences
docs.text:
The JsonPreprocessor supports the explicit embedding of binary values (in hexadecimal escape notation):

"bytesequence" : b'\x52\x6f\x62\x6f\x74\x46\x72\x61\x6d\x65\x77\x6f\x72\x6b\x20\x41\x49\x4f'

The result is the resolved content of Python type bytes:

DotDict({'bytesequence': b'RobotFramework AIO'})

Warning

This feature requires single quotes: b'...'. Double quotes must not be used.

docs.text: The complete JSONP syntax on one page. Click on a feature to get the details.

docs.text: Expression Meaning [1], [${intparam}] list index (integer) ['keyname'], [${stringparam}], ['${stringparam}'] dictionary key (string) ['${intparam}'] integer parameter converted to a dictionary key (string)
