docs.title: Line comments
docs.text:
Comments can be added to JSONP files with //:

{
   // JSON keywords
   "param_06" : true,
   "param_07" : false,
   "param_08" : null,
   // Python keywords
   "param_09" : True,
   "param_10" : False,
   "param_11" : None
}

All lines starting with // are ignored by the JsonPreprocessor. The output of this example is the same as in section Boolean and null values.

docs.title: Block comments and inline comments
docs.text:
Block comments and inline comments are realized by a pair of /* */:

{
   /*
   "param1" : 1,
   "param2" : "A",
   */

   "testlist" : ["A1", /*"B2", "C3",*/ "D4"]
}

Outcome:

{'testlist': ['A1', 'D4']}

Good practice

Use comments to explain the meaning of a parameter, its unit or the range of valid values - especially in files that are maintained by several people.

{
   // timeout for the connection to the device, in seconds (valid: 1..120)
   "connect_timeout" : 30
}

docs.title: Two notations for the same thing
docs.text:
Up to now we have accessed dictionary keys in the standard notation:

${dictionary}['key']['sub_key']

Additionally, the JsonPreprocessor supports the so called dotdict notation where keys are handled as attributes:

${dictionary.key.sub_key}
Standard notation dotdict notation Syntax ${dictionary}['key']['sub_key'] ${dictionary.key.sub_key} Position of keys in square brackets, outside the curly brackets separated by dots, inside the curly brackets Dots in key names allowed not allowed List indices [0] .0 Readability of deeply nested expressions good decreases quickly

docs.title: Dots inside key names
docs.text:
In standard notation key names are allowed to contain dots:

${dictionary}['key']['sub.key']

In dotdict notation this would cause ambiguities:

${dictionary.key.sub.key}

Therefore this is not possible! If you need dots inside key names, you must use the standard notation.

Recommendation

Prefer underscores as separator inside key names - like done in all examples in this documentation. Do you really need dots inside key names?

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
In the following example we create a composite data structure and access single elements in both notations:

{
   // composite data structure
   "params" : [{"dict_1_key_1" : "dict_1_key_1 value",
                "dict_1_key_2" : ["dict_1_key_2 value 1", "dict_1_key_2 value 2"]},
               //
               {"dict_2_key_1" : "dict_2_key_1 value",
                "dict_2_key_2" : {"dict_2_A_key_1" : "dict_2_A_key_1 value",
                                  "dict_2_A_key_2" : ["dict_2_A_key_2 value 1", "dict_2_A_key_2 value 2"]}}],
   //
   // access to single elements of composite data structure
   //
   // a) standard notation
   "dict_1_key_2_value_2_standard" : ${params}[0]['dict_1_key_2'][1],
   // b) dotdict notation
   "dict_1_key_2_value_2_dotdict" : ${params.0.dict_1_key_2.1},
   //
   // c) standard notation
   "dict_2_A_key_2_value_2_standard" : ${params}[1]['dict_2_key_2']['dict_2_A_key_2'][1],
   // d) dotdict notation
   "dict_2_A_key_2_value_2_dotdict" : ${params.1.dict_2_key_2.dict_2_A_key_2.1}
}

Outcome:

{'dict_1_key_2_value_2_dotdict': 'dict_1_key_2 value 2',
 'dict_1_key_2_value_2_standard': 'dict_1_key_2 value 2',
 'dict_2_A_key_2_value_2_dotdict': 'dict_2_A_key_2 value 2',
 'dict_2_A_key_2_value_2_standard': 'dict_2_A_key_2 value 2',
 'params': [{'dict_1_key_1': 'dict_1_key_1 value',
             'dict_1_key_2': ['dict_1_key_2 value 1', 'dict_1_key_2 value 2']},
            {'dict_2_key_1': 'dict_2_key_1 value',
             'dict_2_key_2': {'dict_2_A_key_1': 'dict_2_A_key_1 value',
                              'dict_2_A_key_2': ['dict_2_A_key_2 value 1',
                                                 'dict_2_A_key_2 value 2']}}]}

Keep it readable

The dotdict notation is a reduced one. Because parts are missing (e.g. the single quotes around key names), the outcome can be code that is hard to understand. When the data structure becomes more and more nested (and if also the key names contain numbers), expressions like ${params.1.dict_2_key_2.dict_2_A_key_2.1} become challenging. In such cases prefer the standard notation.

docs.title: dotdict access in Python
docs.text:
Independent from the notation inside the JSONP file, the returned DotDict supports the dot notation also in Python:

values = CJsonPreprocessor().jsonLoad("./config.jsonp")
print(values.params[1].dict_2_key_2.dict_2_A_key_1)

docs.title: Dynamic key names
docs.text:
In section Overwriting parameters we defined the value of string parameters dynamically:

"str_val"   : "ABC",
"newparam1" : "prefix_${str_val}_suffix",

The same is possible at the left-hand side of the colon. In this case the name of the key that shall be overwritten is created dynamically.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
"strval"  : "A",
"dictval" : {"A_2" : 1},
${dictval}['${strval}_2'] : 2

The second line defines a dictionary with the key A_2. The third line overwrites the initial value of this key. The name of this key is composed with the help of the parameter strval.

Outcome:

{'dictval': {'A_2': 2}, 'strval': 'A'}

The same in dotdict notation:

"strval"  : "A",
"dictval" : {"A_2" : 1},
${dictval.${strval}_2} : 3

docs.title: Precondition: the key must exist
docs.text:
Warning

The precondition for using dynamic key names is that a key with the resulting name (here A_2) already exists. Therefore this mechanism can be used to overwrite the value of existing keys, but not to create new keys!

This does not work, because dollar operator expressions are not allowed within the key names of a dictionary definition:

"strval"  : "A",
"dictval" : {"${strval}_2" : 1}

Outcome:

A substitution in key names is not allowed! Please update the key name "${strval}_2"

flowchart LR
    Q{"Does the key<br/>${strval}_2 = 'A_2'<br/>already exist?"}
    Q -- yes --> OK["value is overwritten"]
    Q -- no --> ERR["error"]

docs.title: From explicit to implicit
docs.text:
Up to now we have discussed two different ways of creating nested dictionaries.

The first one is "on the fly":

{
   "project_values" : {"keyA" : "keyA value",
                       "keyB" : {"keyB1" : "keyB1 value",
                                 "keyB2" : {"keyB21" : "keyB21 value",
                                            "keyB22" : "keyB22 value"}}}
}

If the definition has to be split (e.g. into several files), we have to add keys - and also the initialization - line by line:

{
   "project_values" : {},
   ${project_values}['keyA'] : "keyA value",
   ${project_values}['keyB'] : {},
   ${project_values}['keyB']['keyB1'] : "keyB1 value",
   ${project_values}['keyB']['keyB2'] : {},
   ${project_values}['keyB']['keyB2']['keyB21'] : "keyB21 value",
   ${project_values}['keyB']['keyB2']['keyB22'] : "keyB22 value"
}

The result is the same as in the previous example. But this way is long-winded, because every initialization of a dictionary requires a separate line of code (at every level).

To shorten the code, the JsonPreprocessor supports the implicit creation of dictionaries. Missing levels are created automatically:

Standard notationdotdict notation 
{
   ${project_values}['keyA'] : "keyA value",
   ${project_values}['keyB']['keyB1'] : "keyB1 value",
   ${project_values}['keyB']['keyB2']['keyB21'] : "keyB21 value",
   ${project_values}['keyB']['keyB2']['keyB22'] : "keyB22 value"
}

{
   ${project_values.keyA} : "keyA value",
   ${project_values.keyB.keyB1} : "keyB1 value",
   ${project_values.keyB.keyB2.keyB21} : "keyB21 value",
   ${project_values.keyB.keyB2.keyB22} : "keyB22 value"
}

(Precondition: no key name contains a dot.)

Caution

  • Do not mix both notations in one line of code. If lists and numerical indices are involved, prefer the standard notation.
  • In case of a missing level in between - like in ${project_values.keyB.keyB2.keyB22} : "keyB22 value" - you will not get an error message! The entire data structure is created implicitly. This makes the mechanism very susceptible to typing mistakes.
  • The implicit creation does not work with lists. A list index out of range causes an error.

docs.title: Key names are hard coded
docs.text:
The implicit creation of data structures is only possible with hard coded key names. Parameters are not supported.

{
   "paramA" : "ABC",
   "subKey" : "ABC",
   ${testdict.subKey.subKey.paramA} : "DEF"
}

All sub key levels within the expression ${testdict.subKey.subKey.paramA} are interpreted as hard coded strings, even if parameters with the same name exist. The name of the implicitly created key at bottom level is "paramA" - and not the value "ABC" of the parameter with the same name.

Outcome:

{'paramA': 'ABC', 'subKey': 'ABC', 'testdict': {'subKey': {'subKey': {'paramA': 'DEF'}}}}

docs.title: Parameters may refer to existing keys
docs.text:
It is possible to use parameters to refer to already existing keys:

{
   // <data structure created implicitly>
   ${testdict.subKey_1.subKey_2.subKey_3} : "ABC",

   // <string parameter with name of an existing key>
   "keyName_3" : "subKey_3",

   // <parameter used to refer to an existing key>
   ${testdict.subKey_1.subKey_2.${keyName_3}} : "XYZ"
}

Outcome:

{'keyName_3': 'subKey_3',
 'testdict': {'subKey_1': {'subKey_2': {'subKey_3': 'XYZ'}}}}

docs.title: Parameters cannot create new keys
docs.text:
{
   // <data structure created implicitly>
   ${testdict.subKey_1.subKey_2.subKey_3} : "ABC",

   // <string parameter with name of a not existing key>
   "keyName_4" : "subKey_4",

   // <usage of keyName_4 is not possible here>
   ${testdict.subKey_1.subKey_2.${keyName_4}} : "XYZ"
}

Outcome is the following error:

Identified dynamic name of key '${testdict.subKey_1.subKey_2.${keyName_4}}' that does not exist.
But new keys can only be created based on hard code names.

The same error happens with the standard notation:

${testdict}['subKey_1']['subKey_2'][${keyName_4}] : "XYZ"

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    S["${a.b.c} : value"] --> L{"Does every level<br/>already exist?"}
    L -- yes --> W["value is overwritten"]
    L -- no --> H{"Are the missing levels<br/>hard coded key names?"}
    H -- yes --> C["missing dictionaries are created"]
    H -- "no (parameter)" --> E["error"]

docs.title: The scenario
docs.text:
A software component A requires a set of configuration parameters. A software component B, that belongs to the same project, requires another set of configuration parameters. Additionally both components require a common set of parameters (with the same values).

Without imports, both JSON files would contain the common set of parameters. This is unfavorable, because the corresponding values need to be maintained at two different positions.

Therefore we use three files:

  1. common.jsonp containing all parameters that are the same for component A and component B
  2. componentA.jsonp containing the remaining parameters required for component A
  3. componentB.jsonp containing the remaining parameters required for component B
flowchart LR
    common["common.jsonp"]
    A["componentA.jsonp"]
    B["componentB.jsonp"]
    common -- "[import]" --> A
    common -- "[import]" --> B

docs.title: The import key
Multiple imports of the same file
docs.text:
A JSONP file can be imported more than once anywhere in the set of JSONP configuration files. This mechanism can be used to define a common part for different subkeys.

common_config/common.jsonpcomponentA.jsonp 
{
   // common parameters
   "common_param_1" : "common value 1",
   "common_param_2" : "common value 2"
}

{
   // component A parameters
   "componentA_param_1" : {
                             "componentA_param_1_a" : "componentA_param_1_a value",
                             // common parameters within componentA_param_1
                             "[import]"             : "./common_config/common.jsonp",
                             "componentA_param_1_b" : "componentA_param_1_b value"
                          },
   "componentA_param_2" : {
                             "componentA_param_2_a" : "componentA_param_2_a value",
                             // common parameters within componentA_param_2
                             "[import]"             : "./common_config/common.jsonp",
                             "componentA_param_2_b" : "componentA_param_2_b value"
                          }
}

Outcome: The content of common.jsonp is part of componentA_param_1 and also part of componentA_param_2.

{'componentA_param_1': {'common_param_1': 'common value 1',
                        'common_param_2': 'common value 2',
                        'componentA_param_1_a': 'componentA_param_1_a value',
                        'componentA_param_1_b': 'componentA_param_1_b value'},
 'componentA_param_2': {'common_param_1': 'common value 1',
                        'common_param_2': 'common value 2',
                        'componentA_param_2_a': 'componentA_param_2_a value',
                        'componentA_param_2_b': 'componentA_param_2_b value'}}

docs.title: Dynamic import paths
docs.text:
The values of "[import]" keys must be of type str. Therefore it is possible to use dollar operator expressions inside import paths.

An alternative version of the file componentA.jsonp from the example above:

{
   "common_config_dir"  : "./common_config",
   // component A parameters
   "componentA_param_1" : {
                             "componentA_param_1_a" : "componentA_param_1_a value",
                             // common parameters within componentA_param_1
                             "[import]"             : "${common_config_dir}/common.jsonp",
                             "componentA_param_1_b" : "componentA_param_1_b value"
                          },
   "componentA_param_2" : {
                             "componentA_param_2_a" : "componentA_param_2_a value",
                             // common parameters within componentA_param_2
                             "[import]"             : "${common_config_dir}/common.jsonp",
                             "componentA_param_2_b" : "componentA_param_2_b value"
                          }
}

The outcome is the same as in the previous example.

Tip

The import path can also be computed with Python inline code, e.g. to select a file depending on a condition. For conditions the import object is the better readable alternative.

docs.title: Optional imports
docs.text:
The key "[import?]" imports a JSON file only if the file exists. A not existing file is silently ignored.

{
   "[import]"  : "./common.jsonp",
   // local settings of a developer; not part of the repository
   "[import?]" : "./local_overrides.jsonp"
}
  • The value must be of type str. Dollar operator expressions are allowed, like in "[import]".
  • Only the existence of the file is optional. An existing file with a syntax error, a not available parameter inside the path and a cyclic import are still errors.
  • Optional imports are possible in all levels, also within imported files and sub-objects. optional is not inherited: a normal "[import]" of a not existing file inside an optionally imported file is still an error.
  • "[import?]" is a short form of an import object with "optional" : true.

docs.title: Conditional imports
docs.text:
Instead of a path, the value of an "[import]" key can be an import object with the following keys:

Key Required Value file yes path of the file to import (str, dollar operator expressions allowed) if no condition (bool): the file is imported only if the condition is true else no (requires if) path of the file to import if the condition is false optional no literal true or false (default): a not existing file (file or else) is ignored 
{
   "target"    : "bench1",
   "use_debug" : true,
   "[import]"  : {
                    "file" : "./debug.jsonp",
                    "if"   : ${use_debug},
                    "else" : "./release.jsonp"
                 },
   "[import]"  : {
                    "file"     : "./benches/${target}.jsonp",
                    "if"       : <<${target} in ["bench1", "bench2"]>>,
                    "optional" : true
                 }
}

The condition can be:

  • a boolean literal: true, false, True, False,
  • a parameter of type bool: ${use_debug}, ${config.debug}, ${config}['debug'],
  • Python inline code that returns a bool: <<${hw_revision} >= 3>>.
flowchart TD
    start(["[import] object"]) --> hasIf{"key 'if'?"}
    hasIf -- no --> file["path = file"]
    hasIf -- yes --> cond{"condition"}
    cond -- true --> file
    cond -- false --> hasElse{"key 'else'?"}
    hasElse -- no --> skip(["nothing is imported"])
    hasElse -- yes --> other["path = else"]
    file --> exists{"file exists?"}
    other --> exists
    exists -- yes --> import(["file is imported"])
    exists -- no --> opt{"optional?"}
    opt -- true --> skip
    opt -- false --> error(["error: file is not existing"])

Note

The condition is evaluated like any other value. It is recommended to define the parameters used in a condition before the import. Imported values overwrite previously defined values with the same name, like in a normal import.

Strings in inline code

Use <<${target} == "bench1">>, not <<"${target}" == "bench1">>. The dollar operator expression already provides a string value. See Python inline code.

docs.title: Rules and restrictions
docs.text: Rule Details Content of an imported file must be a JSON object ({ ... }) Not existing file causes an error File '...' is not existing! (except with "[import?]" or "optional" : true) Cyclic imports are detected and cause an error (Cyclic import detection: ...) Environment variables are allowed in import paths in the notation of the operating system, e.g. %CONFIG_DIR%/common.jsonp on Windows Value of "[import?]" must be of type str; an import object is not allowed (use "optional" : true instead) Keys of an import object only file, if, else and optional are allowed, each key only once Value of if must be of type bool (true, false, parameter or inline code); "true" (string) is an error Value of optional must be the literal true or false; parameters are not allowed

docs.title: The JSONP format - overview
docs.text: This chapter explains the format of JSONP files in detail - step by step, from plain JSON to the advanced features. We concentrate on the content of the JSONP files and the corresponding results, available as Python dictionary.

docs.title: Learning path
docs.text:
The sections build on each other. If you are new to JSONP, read them in this order:

flowchart LR
    subgraph basics["Basics"]
        direction TB
        A[Standard JSON] --> B[Boolean and null values] --> C[Comments]
    end
    subgraph structure["Structuring"]
        direction TB
        D[Import of JSON files] --> E[Overwriting parameters]
    end
    subgraph advanced["Advanced"]
        direction TB
        F[dotdict notation] --> G[Dynamic key names] --> H[Implicit creation of dictionaries] --> I[Python inline code]
    end
    subgraph details["Details"]
        direction TB
        J[Special characters] --> K[Byte sequences]
    end
    basics --> structure --> advanced --> details
Section You learn ... Standard JSON format that every valid JSON file is also a valid JSONP file Boolean and null values to use true/True, false/False, null/None Comments to document your configuration with // and /* */ Import of JSON files to split a configuration into several files Overwriting parameters to reference and to change existing values with ${...} dotdict notation a shorter notation to access nested values Dynamic key names to address keys by means of parameters Implicit creation of dictionaries to create nested dictionaries in one line Python inline code to compute values with Python expressions <<...>> Special characters within key names which characters are not allowed in key names Byte sequences to embed binary values

The Cheat sheet summarizes the complete syntax on one page.

docs.title: The basic idea: the dollar operator
docs.text:
Most of the JSONP features are built around one single syntax element - the dollar operator ${...}. It refers to a parameter that is defined somewhere in the JSONP file (or in an imported file).

{
   "name"     : "World",
   "greeting" : "Hello ${name}!",      // right-hand side: read a value
   ${name}    : "JSONP"                // left-hand side: overwrite a value
}
Position Meaning Example Right-hand side of the colon, without quotes value with original data type "b" : ${a} Right-hand side of the colon, inside quotes value converted to string "b" : "prefix_${a}" Left-hand side of the colon (never in quotes) overwrite or create a value ${a} : 1

docs.title: How to read the examples
docs.text:
• Every example can be executed with the script from the Quick start.
  • Some examples show only a part of a JSONP file (without the outer curly brackets).
  • The outcome is shown in the format of Python's pprint for dictionaries (keys sorted alphabetically). The real return value is a DotDict, see Standard JSON format.

JSONP in RobotFramework AIO

The JSONP format is also used within the test automation framework RobotFramework AIO (homepage). The component that executes the JsonPreprocessor there is called TestsuitesManagement. Because Robot Framework has its own syntax rules, the JSONP format deviates in some cases in both worlds. Where this is the case, you find a corresponding hint.

docs.title: Overwriting parameters
docs.text:
This section is the heart of the JSONP format. It answers the following questions:

  1. How to change a value that was defined in an imported file?
  2. How to get the value of an already existing parameter?
  3. How to get the value of a single element of a list or a dictionary?
  4. How to overwrite the value of a single element of a list or a dictionary?
  5. How to add an element to a dictionary?

docs.title: Overwrite a value defined in an imported file
docs.text:
We take over the scenario from section Import of JSON files. But now component B requires a different value of a common parameter.

common.jsonpcomponentB.jsonp 
{
   // common parameters
   "common_param_1" : "common value 1",
   "common_param_2" : "common value 2"
}

{
   // common parameters
   "[import]" : "./common.jsonp",
   //
   // component B parameters
   "componentB_param_1" : "componentB value 1",
   "componentB_param_2" : "componentB value 2",
   // overwrite parameter initialized by imported file
   "common_param_2" : "common componentB value 2"
}

With "common_param_2" : "common componentB value 2" in componentB.jsonp, the initial definition "common_param_2" : "common value 2" in common.jsonp is overwritten.

Outcome:

{'common_param_1': 'common value 1',
 'common_param_2': 'common componentB value 2',
 'componentB_param_1': 'componentB value 1',
 'componentB_param_2': 'componentB value 2'}

docs.title: The order matters
docs.text:
Important

The value a parameter has finally, depends on the order of definitions, redefinitions and imports!

In file componentB.jsonp we move the import of common.jsonp to the bottom:

{
   // component B parameters
   "componentB_param_1" : "componentB value 1",
   "componentB_param_2" : "componentB value 2",
   "common_param_2"     : "common componentB value 2",
   //
   // common parameters
   "[import]" : "./common.jsonp"
}

Now the imported file overwrites the value initialized in the importing file.

Outcome:

{'common_param_1': 'common value 1',
 'common_param_2': 'common value 2',
 'componentB_param_1': 'componentB value 1',
 'componentB_param_2': 'componentB value 2'}

flowchart TB
    subgraph top["Import at the top"]
        direction TB
        t1["import common.jsonp<br/>common_param_2 = 'common value 2'"] --> t2["common_param_2 = 'common componentB value 2'"]
        t2 --> t3(["Result: 'common componentB value 2'"])
    end
    subgraph bottom["Import at the bottom"]
        direction TB
        b1["common_param_2 = 'common componentB value 2'"] --> b2["import common.jsonp<br/>common_param_2 = 'common value 2'"]
        b2 --> b3(["Result: 'common value 2'"])
    end

Rule of thumb: the definition that is processed last wins - like in a program that assigns a variable several times.

docs.title: Access existing parameters
docs.text:
Up to now we considered simple data types only. In the following examples all values are part of composite data types like lists and dictionaries:

common.jsonpcomponentB.jsonp 
{
   // common parameters
   "common_param_1" : ["common value 1.1", "common value 1.2"],
   "common_param_2" : {"common_key_2_1" : "common value 2.1" ,
                       "common_key_2_2" : "common value 2.2"}
}

{
   // common parameters
   "[import]" : "./common.jsonp",
   //
   // component B parameters
   "componentB_param_1" : ["componentB value 1.1", "componentB value 1.2"],
   "componentB_param_2" : {"componentB_key_2_1" : "componentB value 2.1" ,
                           "componentB_key_2_2" : "componentB value 2.2"}
}

We introduce a new file componentB.2.jsonp that imports componentB.jsonp and creates new parameters based on already existing parameters:

{
   // import of componentB parameters
   "[import]" : "./componentB.jsonp",
   //
   // some additional parameters of simple data type
   "string_val" : "ABC",
   "int_val"    : 123,
   "float_val"  : 4.56,
   "bool_val"   : true,
   "null_val"   : null,

   // access to existing parameters
   "string_val_b"         : ${string_val},
   "int_val_b"            : ${int_val},
   "float_val_b"          : ${float_val},
   "bool_val_b"           : ${bool_val},
   "null_val_b"           : ${null_val},
   "common_param_1_b"     : ${common_param_1},
   "componentB_param_2_b" : ${componentB_param_2}
}

Outcome:

{'bool_val': True,
 'bool_val_b': True,
 'common_param_1': ['common value 1.1', 'common value 1.2'],
 'common_param_1_b': ['common value 1.1', 'common value 1.2'],
 'common_param_2': {'common_key_2_1': 'common value 2.1',
                    'common_key_2_2': 'common value 2.2'},
 'componentB_param_1': ['componentB value 1.1', 'componentB value 1.2'],
 'componentB_param_2': {'componentB_key_2_1': 'componentB value 2.1',
                        'componentB_key_2_2': 'componentB value 2.2'},
 'componentB_param_2_b': {'componentB_key_2_1': 'componentB value 2.1',
                          'componentB_key_2_2': 'componentB value 2.2'},
 'float_val': 4.56,
 'float_val_b': 4.56,
 'int_val': 123,
 'int_val_b': 123,
 'null_val': None,
 'null_val_b': None,
 'string_val': 'ABC',
 'string_val_b': 'ABC'}

Rules for accessing parameters

  • Existing parameters are accessed by a dollar operator and a pair of curly brackets (${...}) with the parameter name inside.
  • If the entire expression at the right-hand side of the colon is such a dollar operator expression, it is not required to encapsulate this expression in quotes (in opposite to what pure JSON would require).
  • Without quotes, the dollar operator keeps the data type of the referenced parameter. With quotes, the value is converted to type str. This implicit string conversion is limited to parameters of simple data types. Composite data types like lists and dictionaries cannot be used for that.

docs.title: With or without quotes
docs.text:
The dollar operator keeps the data type of the referenced parameter. If int_val is of type int, also int_val_b is of type int:

"int_val_b" : ${int_val},

With quotes, the parameter int_val_b is of type str:

"int_val_b" : "${int_val}",

docs.title: Composite strings
docs.text:
Further content can be added between the double quotes. This can be used to create composite strings:

"str_val"   : "ABC",
"int_val"   : 1,
"float_val" : 2.3,
"bool_val"  : True,
"none_val"  : None,
"list_val"  : [1,2,3],
"dict_val"  : {"A" : "B"},
"newparam1" : "prefix_${str_val}_suffix",
"newparam2" : "prefix_${int_val}_suffix",
"newparam3" : "prefix_${float_val}_suffix",
"newparam4" : "prefix_${bool_val}_suffix",
"newparam5" : "prefix_${none_val}_suffix"

Outcome:

{'bool_val': True,
 'dict_val': {'A': 'B'},
 'float_val': 2.3,
 'int_val': 1,
 'list_val': [1, 2, 3],
 'newparam1': 'prefix_ABC_suffix',
 'newparam2': 'prefix_1_suffix',
 'newparam3': 'prefix_2.3_suffix',
 'newparam4': 'prefix_True_suffix',
 'newparam5': 'prefix_None_suffix',
 'none_val': None,
 'str_val': 'ABC'}

Using composite data types inside strings is not supported:

"newparam6" : "prefix_${list_val}_suffix",
"newparam7" : "prefix_${dict_val}_suffix"

Result for "newparam6":

The substitution of parameter '${list_val}' inside the string value 'prefix_${list_val}_suffix' is not allowed!
Composite data types like lists and dictionaries cannot be substituted inside strings.

docs.title: Access a single element
docs.text:
To access an element of a list and a key of a dictionary, we change the content of file componentB.2.jsonp to:

{
   // import of componentB parameters
   "[import]" : "./componentB.jsonp",
   //
   "list_element_0" : ${componentB_param_1}[0],
   "dict_key_2_2"   : ${common_param_2}['common_key_2_2']
}

Outcome:

{'common_param_1': ['common value 1.1', 'common value 1.2'],
 'common_param_2': {'common_key_2_1': 'common value 2.1',
                    'common_key_2_2': 'common value 2.2'},
 'componentB_param_1': ['componentB value 1.1', 'componentB value 1.2'],
 'componentB_param_2': {'componentB_key_2_1': 'componentB value 2.1',
                        'componentB_key_2_2': 'componentB value 2.2'},
 'dict_key_2_2': 'common value 2.2',
 'list_element_0': 'componentB value 1.1'}

docs.title: Overwrite a single element
docs.text:
In the next example we overwrite the value of a list element and the value of a dictionary key:

{
   // import of componentB parameters
   "[import]" : "./componentB.jsonp",
   //
   ${componentB_param_1}[0]            : "componentB value 1.1 (new)",
   ${common_param_2}['common_key_2_1'] : "common value 2.1 (new)"
}

The dollar operator syntax at the left-hand side of the colon is the same as previously used on the right-hand side.

Warning

The entire expression at the left-hand side of the colon must not be encapsulated in quotes.

Outcome: The single elements of the list and the dictionary are updated, all other elements are unchanged.

{'common_param_1': ['common value 1.1', 'common value 1.2'],
 'common_param_2': {'common_key_2_1': 'common value 2.1 (new)',
                    'common_key_2_2': 'common value 2.2'},
 'componentB_param_1': ['componentB value 1.1 (new)', 'componentB value 1.2'],
 'componentB_param_2': {'componentB_key_2_1': 'componentB value 2.1',
                        'componentB_key_2_2': 'componentB value 2.2'}}

docs.title: Add an element
docs.text:
Adding further elements to an already existing list is not possible! But it is possible to add keys to an already existing dictionary.

The following example extends the dictionary common_param_2 by an additional key common_key_2_3:

{
   // import of componentB parameters
   "[import]" : "./componentB.jsonp",
   //
   ${common_param_2}['common_key_2_3'] : "common value 2.3"
}

Outcome:

{'common_param_1': ['common value 1.1', 'common value 1.2'],
 'common_param_2': {'common_key_2_1': 'common value 2.1',
                    'common_key_2_2': 'common value 2.2',
                    'common_key_2_3': 'common value 2.3'},
 'componentB_param_1': ['componentB value 1.1', 'componentB value 1.2'],
 'componentB_param_2': {'componentB_key_2_1': 'componentB value 2.1',
                        'componentB_key_2_2': 'componentB value 2.2'}}

Need a longer list?

Overwrite the entire list instead, e.g. with Python inline code: ${componentB_param_1} : <<${componentB_param_1} + ["new element"]>>.

docs.title: Dictionary keys and indices as parameter
docs.text:
In all examples above the indices of lists and the key names of dictionaries are hard coded. It is also possible to use parameters. The following example swaps the elements of a list and the values of a dictionary:

{
   "index1"               : 0,
   "index2"               : 1,
   "key1"                 : "keyA",
   "key2"                 : "keyB",
   "testlist"             : ["A", "B"],
   "testdict"             : {"keyA" : "A", "keyB" : "B"},
   "tmp1"                 : ${testlist}[${index1}],
   "tmp2"                 : ${testdict}[${key1}],
   ${testlist}[${index1}] : ${testlist}[${index2}],
   ${testdict}[${key1}]   : ${testdict}[${key2}],
   ${testlist}[${index2}] : ${tmp1},
   ${testdict}[${key2}]   : ${tmp2}
}

Outcome:

{'index1': 0,
 'index2': 1,
 'key1': 'keyA',
 'key2': 'keyB',
 'testdict': {'keyA': 'B', 'keyB': 'A'},
 'testlist': ['B', 'A'],
 'tmp1': 'A',
 'tmp2': 'A'}

docs.title: Meaning of single quotes in square brackets
docs.text:
Single quotes convert the content inside to a string.

  • If the parameter param is of type str, the expressions [${param}] and ['${param}'] have the same outcome: the content inside the square brackets is a string.
  • If the parameter param is of type int, the quotes in ['${param}'] convert the integer value to a string. Without the quotes ([${param}]), the content inside the square brackets is an integer.

Only strings and integers are expected inside square brackets. Dictionaries require a string (a key name), lists require an integer (an index). Deviations cause an error.

Summarized, the following combinations are valid (on both sides of the colon):

Expression Container Index / key ${listparam}[${intparam}] list integer parameter ${listparam}[1] list integer literal ${dictparam}['${intparam}'] dictionary integer parameter converted to string ${dictparam}[${stringparam}] dictionary string parameter ${dictparam}['${stringparam}'] dictionary string parameter ${dictparam}['keyname'] dictionary string literal

docs.title: Use of a common dictionary
docs.text:
The last example in this section covers the following use case:

  • A project has several JSONP files, each for a certain purpose (e.g. one file per feature).
  • They are all imported into a main JSONP file - the file that is handed over to the JsonPreprocessor.
  • Every imported file introduces a bunch of parameters. All parameters shall be part of one common dictionary.
flowchart LR
    A["featureA.jsonp"] -- "[import]" --> P["project.jsonp"]
    B["featureB.jsonp"] -- "[import]" --> P
    C["featureC.jsonp"] -- "[import]" --> P
    P --> R[("project_values<br/>common · featureA_params ·<br/>featureB_params · featureC_params")]
project.jsonpfeatureA.jsonpfeatureB.jsonpfeatureC.jsonp 
{
   // define some common values
   ${project_values}['common_project_param_1'] : "common project value 1",
   ${project_values}['common_project_param_2'] : "common project value 2",
   //
   // import feature parameters
   "[import]" : "./featureA.jsonp",
   "[import]" : "./featureB.jsonp",
   "[import]" : "./featureC.jsonp"
}

{
   // parameters required for feature A
   ${project_values}['featureA_params']['featureA_param_1'] : "featureA param 1 value",
   ${project_values}['featureA_params']['featureA_param_2'] : "featureA param 2 value"
}

{
   // parameters required for feature B
   ${project_values}['featureB_params']['featureB_param_1'] : "featureB param 1 value",
   ${project_values}['featureB_params']['featureB_param_2'] : "featureB param 2 value"
}

{
   // parameters required for feature C
   ${project_values}['featureC_params']['featureC_param_1'] : "featureC param 1 value",
   ${project_values}['featureC_params']['featureC_param_2'] : "featureC param 2 value"
}

It is not required to start with dictionary initializations like

"project_values" : {},
${project_values}['featureA_params'] : {},
${project_values}['featureB_params'] : {},
${project_values}['featureC_params'] : {},

These initializations are done implicitly by the JsonPreprocessor, see Implicit creation of dictionaries.

Warning

It is still possible to initialize a dictionary explicitly with {}. But keep in mind: this deletes all already existing keys in this dictionary!

Outcome:

{'project_values': {'common_project_param_1': 'common project value 1',
                    'common_project_param_2': 'common project value 2',
                    'featureA_params': {'featureA_param_1': 'featureA param 1 value',
                                        'featureA_param_2': 'featureA param 2 value'},
                    'featureB_params': {'featureB_param_1': 'featureB param 1 value',
                                        'featureB_param_2': 'featureB param 2 value'},
                    'featureC_params': {'featureC_param_1': 'featureC param 1 value',
                                        'featureC_param_2': 'featureC param 2 value'}}}

docs.title: Motivation
docs.text:
It might be required to have access to Python builtin functions, e.g. for combining multiple lists into a single list. In pure Python:

A = [1,2,3]
B = [4,5,6]
C = A + B
print(C)      # [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]

In JSONP files, the implementation looks as follows:

"A" : [1,2,3],
"B" : [4,5,6],
"C" : <<${A} + ${B}>>

The expression ${A} + ${B} is handled as Python inline code. Dollar operator expressions can be used inside Python inline code to access any other parameter defined in the JSONP files.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
<<(Python expression)>>

The result of the expression must be of a data type that is supported by JSON: str, int, float, bool, None, list or dict.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
Not allowed Example Inside strings "param" : "The value is <<1 + 1>>" In key names (left-hand side of the colon) <<"key" + "1">> : 1 Directly as index of a value to be overwritten ${param}[<<0 if True else 1>>] : 4 As element of a list "param" : [<<1 + 1>>, 3] Inside a dollar operator expression ${<<"name">>}

The usage of Python inline code is limited to the right-hand side of the colon (key values).

Workaround for indices: compute the index in a separate parameter first:

"param" : [1,2,3],
"index" : <<0 if True else 1>>,
${param}[${index}] : 4

docs.title: Further examples
docs.text:
Create a list of dictionary keys:

"dict"     : {"kA" : "vA", "kB" : "vB"},
"key_list" : <<list(${dict}.keys())>>

Outcome:

{'dict': {'kA': 'vA', 'kB': 'vB'}, 'key_list': ['kA', 'kB']}

Define an import path:

"path_1" : "./file_1.jsonp",
"path_2" : "./file_2.jsonp",
//
"[import]" : <<${path_1} if True else ${path_2}>>

Extend a list:

"testlist" : [1, 2],
${testlist} : <<${testlist} + [3]>>

Security

Python inline code is executed by the JsonPreprocessor. Only load JSONP files from trusted sources - a JSONP file is as powerful as a Python script.

docs.title: Special characters within key names
docs.text:
Basically, the JsonPreprocessor follows the JSON naming convention for key names: within JSONP files allowed is what JSON allows - with one limitation:

The JSONP format uses square, curly and angle brackets as syntax elements: [, ], {, }, <, >.

These brackets must not be used within key names!

This JSONP code:

{
    "[" : 1,
    "B" : ${[}
}

causes an error, because the brackets inside the dollar operator expression cannot be interpreted.

docs.title: Other special characters
docs.text:
All other special characters can be used:

{
    "$" : 1,
    "B" : ${$}
}

Result:

DotDict({'$': 1, 'B': 1})

docs.title: Backslashes
docs.text:
Strings are handled as raw strings. Therefore masking has no effect:

{
    "\\$" : 1,
    "B" : ${\\$}
}

The backslashes are part of the key name:

DotDict({'\\$': 1, 'B': 1})

Note

The masking requires two backslashes. A single backslash causes a JSON syntax error.

Format deviation in RobotFramework AIO

In opposite to the JsonPreprocessor, the TestsuitesManagement of RobotFramework AIO is more restrictive and does not allow any special characters in parameter names. Names are limited to letters, digits and underscores.

Tip

You can restrict the allowed key names even further by a user defined naming convention.

docs.title: Standard JSON format
docs.text:
The JsonPreprocessor supports JSON files with the standard extension .json and standard content.

JSON file:

{
   "param1" : "value1",
   "param2" : "value2"
}

Outcome:

{'param1': 'value1', 'param2': 'value2'}

A JSON file with the extension .jsonp and the same content produces the same output.

Recommendation

Give every JSON file the extension .jsonp to have a strict separation between the standard and the extended JSON format.

docs.title: Data types
docs.text:
The following example still contains standard JSON content, but with parameters of several different data types (simple and composite):

{
   "param_01" : "string",
   "param_02" : 123,
   "param_03" : 4.56,
   "param_04" : ["A", "B", "C"],
   "param_05" : {"A" : 1, "B" : 2, "C" : 3}
}

Outcome:

{'param_01': 'string',
 'param_02': 123,
 'param_03': 4.56,
 'param_04': ['A', 'B', 'C'],
 'param_05': {'A': 1, 'B': 2, 'C': 3}}
JSON Python string str number (integer) int number (real) float array list object dict (returned as DotDict)

docs.title: The returned dictionary type
docs.text:
The output is of a certain dictionary type named DotDict. It behaves like a normal Python dictionary, but additionally allows to access elements with an object oriented dot notation:

values = CJsonPreprocessor().jsonLoad("./config.jsonp")

values['param_05']['A']   # standard access
values.param_05.A         # dot notation

Details about the corresponding notation inside JSONP files can be found in section dotdict notation.

docs.title: JsonPreprocessor Self-Test (python-jsonpreprocessor/test)
docs.text: All paths in this document are relative to the component root directory python-jsonpreprocessor (e.g. test/testconfig/TestConfig.py).

docs.title: What is this about?
docs.text: JsonPreprocessor is a Python library that extends plain JSON files with additional capabilities (parameter substitution, file imports, inline Python code, comments, etc.). To keep this library reliable, and to make sure that no future change accidentally breaks any existing feature, there is an automated test suite (a "self-test") located under test/.

docs.title: How does the basic principle work?
docs.text:
Think of the test suite as a long checklist of examples:

  • Each example consists of a small sample JSON file (the input) and a clear expectation: "the result must look exactly like this" or "this must be rejected with exactly this error message".
  • A test runner (pytest) automatically works through this checklist from top to bottom, loads every sample file with JsonPreprocessor, and compares the actual result against the expectation.
  • At the end you get a simple number: "278 out of 278 tests passed" (as of the latest additions), or a precise listing of which examples failed and why.

docs.title: What is the checklist made of?
docs.text:
The checklist itself lives in a single file, test/testconfig/TestConfig.py. This is a deliberate design choice: there is only one single source of truth for all test cases, not scattered copies. Each test case has a unique ID (TESTID, e.g. JPP_0001), a description, an expectation, and a reference to a small sample JSON file under test/testfiles/.

In addition to this main checklist, there is a second, smaller test module (test/jpp_test/test_api.py) that doesn't check JSON files, but the library's programming interface itself (e.g. "Can I also load JSON content directly from a text string instead of from a file?").

docs.title: Where can I see the result?
docs.text: For non-programmers, there is a ready-made HTML overview (test/JPP_TestUsecases.html) that lists all test cases from the main checklist as well as the additional API tests in a readable form - with description, expectation, and a link to the respective sample file. This file is automatically generated from the checklist by a small helper script (test/gen_html_overview.py), so it never needs to be maintained by hand.

docs.title: Why does this matter?
docs.text:
• Safety for changes: every code change to JsonPreprocessor can immediately be checked against all ~280 examples.
  • Documentation through examples: the checklist also shows what the library can do (and what it must explicitly reject).
  • Traceability: a failed check shows exactly which example is affected, what was expected, and what actually happened.

docs.title: Section 2: Detailed Information (for application developers and testers)
Directory structure
docs.text:
test/
├── testconfig/
│   ├── TestConfig.py         # single source of truth for all use cases (listofdictUsecases)
│   └── missing_tests.md      # gap analysis: implementation vs. test coverage
├── testfiles/
│   └── jpp-test_config_*.jsonp, import/..., ...
├── jpp_test/
│   ├── conftest.py           # pytest fixtures, path constants
│   ├── comparators.py        # comparison logic (return values / exceptions)
│   ├── test_usecases.py      # data-driven tests sourced from TestConfig.py
│   └── test_api.py           # standalone tests of the public API
├── gen_html_overview.py      # generates JPP_TestUsecases.html
└── JPP_TestUsecases.html     # generated, human readable overview

docs.title: 2.1 test/testconfig/TestConfig.py - the use case database
docs.text:
Contains the list listofdictUsecases. Each entry is a dict with the following keys:

Key Required Meaning TESTID yes Unique ID, e.g. JPP_0275. Numbering convention per SECTION: GOODCASE starts at x00, BADCASE starts at x50. DESCRIPTION yes Short description of the test case. EXPECTATION yes What is expected, in plain text (also shown in the failure report). SECTION / SUBSECTION yes Thematic grouping (e.g. FILE_IMPORTS / BADCASE). JSONFILE yes Relative path to the sample file under test/testfiles/. EXPECTEDEXCEPTION yes (or None) Expected (partial) text of an exception. None means: no exception must be raised. EXPECTEDRETURN yes (or None) Expected pretty-printed representation of the return value. None means: no return value is expected (e.g. because an error is expected instead). HINT, COMMENT optional Additional free-text notes. USERAWPATH optional If True: JSONFILE is resolved relative to test/ instead of relative to testconfig/ (see conftest.py).

If both EXPECTEDEXCEPTION and EXPECTEDRETURN are None, the corresponding test case is skipped in test_usecases.py (pytest.skip, status "UNKNOWN") - a remnant of the former test concept, deliberately kept to allow marking temporarily deactivated cases.

docs.title: 2.2 test/jpp_test/conftest.py - fixtures and path conventions
docs.text:
• Adds test/testconfig to sys.path so that TestConfig.py can be imported.
  • Defines TESTCONFIGPATH (reference path for regular JSONFILE entries) and TESTBASEPATH (reference path for USERAWPATH: True cases).
  • Provides the jpp fixture: a single, session-wide shared CJsonPreprocessor instance. This is deliberate (identical to the former test concept): all ~264 use cases run against the same instance, which also acts as a simple stress test (no hidden side effects between consecutive calls).

docs.title: 2.3 test/jpp_test/comparators.py - comparison logic
docs.text:
Two functions, ported 1:1 from the former component_test.py:

  • analyze_returned_values(EXPECTEDRETURN, dictReturned): compares the pretty-printed lines of the actual return value line by line against the expected text.
  • analyze_exceptions(EXPECTEDEXCEPTION, sException): checks via substring containment (EXPECTEDEXCEPTION in sException), not an exact match. This allows TestConfig.py to specify only the relevant, stable part of an error message, without having to update every test case whenever the wording of an error message changes slightly.

Both functions return a list of error strings (empty list = success), which is then evaluated in test_usecases.py via assert not listErrors.

docs.title: 2.4 test/jpp_test/test_usecases.py - the data-driven test run
docs.text:
• Parametrizes one test function (test_jsonpreprocessor_usecase) with every entry in listofdictUsecases. Each use case appears in the pytest output as its own test case with the ID <TESTID>-<SECTION>-<SUBSECTION> (e.g. JPP_1167-FILE_IMPORTS-BADCASE).
  • Flow per test case:
  • Normalize the JSONFILE path (depending on USERAWPATH).
  • Call jpp.jsonLoad(JSONFILE).
  • Capture the return value or the raised exception.
  • Check both against EXPECTEDRETURN / EXPECTEDEXCEPTION via comparators.py.
  • On mismatch: assert with DESCRIPTION, EXPECTATION, and the concrete error texts in the report - directly copy-pastable into a bug report.

This module fully replaces the former two-layer solution (component_test.py + generated pytest/pytestfiles/* files with subprocess indirection), without touching the data source (TestConfig.py) itself.

docs.title: 2.5 test/jpp_test/test_api.py - public API tests
docs.text:
While test_usecases.py exclusively exercises the file-path-based call jpp.jsonLoad(JSONFILE), test_api.py covers the parts of the public interface that don't fit into this file-based scheme - e.g. alternative constructor parameters or alternative entry points. These are plain, standalone pytest functions (no shared data model like TestConfig.py), covering among others:

  • json_loads() / jsonLoads() - loading JSONP content directly from a string (including the reference_dir parameter for import resolution).
  • json_dump() / jsonDump() - writing a dict back to a JSON file.
  • Constructor parameter current_cfg (pre-seeding the parameter store).
  • Constructor parameter key_pattern (custom regex for valid key names), including validation of the pattern itself (parametrized test for invalid patterns: non-string, empty, .*, whitespace-only).
  • syntax=CSyntaxType.json (strict JSON syntax without the Python keywords True/False/None).
  • getVersion() / getVersionDate().

Every test function carries a short docstring - this is automatically picked up by gen_html_overview.py and used as the description in the HTML overview (see 2.7).

docs.title: 2.6 test/testconfig/missing_tests.md - gap analysis
docs.text:
Documents a systematic comparison of the implementation (JsonPreprocessor/*.py) against test coverage, organized into:

  1. Untested public API methods (now marked [ERLEDIGT]/done, see test_api.py).
  2. Existing error-path code branches without a corresponding test case (now marked [ERLEDIGT]/done, see the associated TESTIDs per row).
  3. Lower-priority edge cases (currently still open).

This file serves as the working basis for future test extensions and should be kept up to date whenever new gaps are identified.

docs.title: 2.7 test/gen_html_overview.py - generated overview
docs.text:
A standalone script (python test/gen_html_overview.py) that generates test/JPP_TestUsecases.html:

  • Section 1 of the HTML file: one row per entry in listofdictUsecases (TestConfig.py), with TESTID, section/subsection (color-coded: green = GOODCASE, red = BADCASE), description, expectation, and a link to the sample file on GitHub.
  • Section 2 of the HTML file: one row per test_* function in test/jpp_test/test_api.py. The list of these functions is not maintained manually, but extracted at generation time directly from the source code of test_api.py via the ast module (function name + docstring) - the overview can therefore never go stale with respect to the test code.
  • At the end, the script prints a short summary to the console, e.g. 264 use case(s) + 11 API test(s) written to '...'. Note: a parametrized API test (test_constructor_rejects_invalid_key_patterns) counts as one row in this overview, but appears as four individual test cases in the pytest run (one per parameter combination) - so "number of rows in the overview" is not necessarily identical to "number of tests executed by pytest".

docs.title: 2.8 Running the tests
docs.text:
cd python-jsonpreprocessor
$env:PYTHONPATH = "<path-to-repo>\python-jsonpreprocessor"
python -m pytest test/jpp_test                       # full suite
python -m pytest test/jpp_test/test_api.py -v         # API tests only
python -m pytest test/jpp_test -k "JPP_1167"          # single use case
python test/gen_html_overview.py                      # regenerate the overview

The API tests are plain, standalone pytest functions (no shared data model like TestConfig.py). No extra configuration step is needed: test/jpp_test/pytest.ini makes pytest automatically discover every test_*.py file under test/jpp_test - so test_api.py is always included whenever test/jpp_test (or the parent test/) is given as the test target. More fine-grained invocation variants:

# a single API test
python -m pytest test/jpp_test/test_api.py::test_json_loads_and_jsonLoads_are_equivalent -v

# a single parameter case of the parametrized test
python -m pytest "test/jpp_test/test_api.py::test_constructor_rejects_invalid_key_patterns[.*-allows key names that are empty]" -v

docs.title: 2.9 Conventions for new test cases
docs.text:
• Always add new use cases to TestConfig.py, never create a copy of the data source.
  • Follow the TESTID numbering convention (GOODCASE starting at x00, BADCASE starting at x50 within the respective SECTION).
  • Keep EXPECTEDEXCEPTION as short as possible, but unambiguous (substring match - see 2.3), so test cases stay robust against small wording changes in the error message.
  • Place new sample files under test/testfiles/, following the same naming scheme (jpp-test_config_<TESTID-digits>.jsonp).
  • After every extension: re-run python test/gen_html_overview.py so the HTML overview stays current.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
In case of any problem the JsonPreprocessor raises an Exception with a meaningful message. There is no partial result - either the complete configuration is valid, or you get an exception.

try:
    values = json_preprocessor.jsonLoad("./file.jsonp")
except Exception as reason:
    print(f"Configuration could not be loaded: {reason}")
    raise

docs.title: Typical errors and how to fix them
docs.text: Message (excerpt) Cause Fix File '...' is not existing! wrong path in jsonLoad or in an "[import]" check the path; relative import paths are relative to the importing file; use "[import?]" for optional files ... [import] object ... invalid import object (unknown key, missing file, else without if, wrong data type) allowed keys: file, if, else, optional; if requires a bool Could not evaluate the condition of the [import] object. the condition refers to a not existing parameter define the parameter before the import Expecting ... : line X column Y with Nearby: '...' JSON syntax error (missing comma, missing quote, ...) the Nearby part shows the text around the error position The parameter '${x}' is not available! reference to a parameter that does not exist check spelling and import order The substitution of parameter '${x}' inside the string value ... is not allowed! a list or dictionary is used inside a string reference the value without quotes, or access a single element A substitution in key names is not allowed! ${...} inside the key of a dictionary definition use dynamic key names on the left-hand side for existing keys Identified dynamic name of key ... that does not exist. a parameter is used to create a new key use hard coded key names for implicit creation Could not set parameter ... list assignment index out of range list index out of range on the left-hand side lists cannot be extended - overwrite the entire list Python inline code must not be ... Python inline code at a not supported position see limitations Cyclic import detection: ... files import each other restructure the imports Key name '...' is invalid. Expected format: '...' key name does not match the key_pattern rename the key, see naming convention

docs.title: Error position in imported files
docs.text:
If an error happens inside an imported file, the message contains the affected file:

Expecting ',' delimiter: line 3 column 4 (char 16)
Nearby: '... {
   "a" : 1
   "b" : 2
}
 ...'
In file: 'C:/project/config/common.jsonp'

Debugging complex configurations

  1. Reduce the configuration step by step (comment out imports with //) until the error disappears.
  2. Use jsonDump to write the resolved result of a working configuration into a standard JSON file and inspect it.

docs.title: User defined naming convention
docs.text:
By default, key names in JSONP files can contain any characters (but cannot be empty). Only the brackets [, ], {, }, <, > must not be used, because they are syntax elements of the JSONP format (see Special characters within key names).

It might be required to add further limitations to the set of allowed characters. For this purpose the JsonPreprocessor supports an optional user defined convention for key names. It is enforced by a regex pattern that is passed to the constructor (parameter key_pattern).

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
Key names may only contain letters, digits and underscores, but must start with a letter:

from JsonPreprocessor.CJsonPreprocessor import CJsonPreprocessor
import pprint

json_preprocessor = CJsonPreprocessor(key_pattern=r'^\p{L}[\p{L}\p{Nd}_]*$')
try:
    values = json_preprocessor.jsonLoad("./file.jsonp")
    pprint.pprint(values)
except Exception as reason:
    print(f"'{reason}'")

The regular expressions \p{L} and \p{Nd} are provided by the regex module:

Expression Matches \p{L} all Unicode characters classified as letter \p{Nd} all Unicode characters classified as decimal digit

A key name that does not match causes an error:

Error: Key name '1st_value' is invalid. Expected format: '^\p{L}[\p{L}\p{Nd}_]*$'

docs.title: Rules for the pattern
docs.text:
Pattern Result not of type str error '' or '.*' error - these patterns would allow empty key names whitespace only error default '.+' every non-empty key name is allowed

RobotFramework AIO

The TestsuitesManagement of RobotFramework AIO uses the convention ^\p{L}[\p{L}\p{Nd}_]*$ for the names of parameters that are made available in Robot Framework.

docs.title: Using the JsonPreprocessor in Python
docs.text:
All functionality is provided by the class CJsonPreprocessor.

from JsonPreprocessor.CJsonPreprocessor import CJsonPreprocessor

flowchart LR
    F[".jsonp file"] -- jsonLoad --> J(["CJsonPreprocessor"])
    S["JSONP string"] -- jsonLoads --> J
    J --> D["DotDict"]
    D -- jsonDump --> O[".json file<br/>(standard JSON)"]

docs.title: Load a JSONP file
docs.text:
The main method is jsonLoad. Input is the path and the name of a JSONP file, output is a dictionary containing all values parsed from this file:

from JsonPreprocessor.CJsonPreprocessor import CJsonPreprocessor
import pprint

json_preprocessor = CJsonPreprocessor()
try:
    values = json_preprocessor.jsonLoad("./file.jsonp")
    pprint.pprint(values)
except Exception as reason:
    print(f"'{reason}'")

About the path:

  • It can be absolute or relative. A relative path is relative to the location of the executed Python script (not to the current working directory).
  • It may contain environment variables, e.g. %CONFIG_DIR%/file.jsonp on Windows.

docs.title: Load JSONP content from a string
docs.text:
If the JSONP content is not available as a file (e.g. it is generated or received from somewhere), use jsonLoads:

content = """
{
   // a comment
   "a" : 1,
   "b" : ${a}
}
"""
values = json_preprocessor.jsonLoads(content)

If the content contains imports with relative paths, pass the directory that shall be used as reference:

values = json_preprocessor.jsonLoads('{"[import]" : "./common.jsonp"}', reference_dir="./config")

docs.title: Write the result as standard JSON
docs.text:
jsonDump writes a dictionary to a file in standard JSON format (all JSONP features resolved) and returns the normalized path:

out_file = json_preprocessor.jsonDump(values, "./resolved_config.json")

This is useful to inspect the final result of a complex set of JSONP files or to hand it over to tools that only understand standard JSON.

docs.title: Constructor options
docs.text: CJsonPreprocessor(syntax=CSyntaxType.python, current_cfg={}, key_pattern=r'.+')

docs.title: Syntax type
docs.text:
Value Meaning CSyntaxType.python (default) Python keywords True, False, None are allowed in JSONP files CSyntaxType.json only the JSON keywords true, false, null are allowed 
from JsonPreprocessor.CJsonPreprocessor import CJsonPreprocessor, CSyntaxType

strict = CJsonPreprocessor(syntax=CSyntaxType.json)

docs.title: Predefined parameters
docs.text:
With current_cfg you can pass parameters that are available in addition to the parameters of the JSONP file. They can be referenced and overwritten in the JSONP file and are part of the result:

json_preprocessor = CJsonPreprocessor(current_cfg={"target" : "Device_01"})
values = json_preprocessor.jsonLoads('{"name" : "${target}_config"}')
# {'target': 'Device_01', 'name': 'Device_01_config'}

docs.title: Key name pattern
docs.text: With key_pattern you can restrict the allowed key names, see User defined naming convention.

docs.title: Method names
docs.text:
All methods are available in two spellings (camel case and snake case). Both are equivalent:

Camel case Snake case jsonLoad json_load jsonLoads json_loads jsonDump json_dump

The complete description of all methods can be found in the API reference.

docs.title: VSCodium support
docs.text:
The JSON syntax extensions introduced by the JsonPreprocessor harm the syntax highlighting of editors:

  • Either the JSON files get the extension .json - then an editor expects a JSON file in standard syntax and marks the extensions as errors,
  • or the extension is changed to .jsonp - but then an editor usually does not know how to display a file of such type.

If you use VSCodium (or Visual Studio Code), you can install the jsonp extension. With this extension the editor displays .jsonp files properly.
